## Keystones

Three, and they are not independent.

### #639 — the policy model (ADR 0009)

Decides whether access capabilities become first-class, what config keys look like, and what composition semantics apply.

Dependants: #603, #604, #609, #680, #687, #691, #706, and PRs #692, #675, #684, #671, #638.

Four contributor PRs are parked behind it, one of them 51 files wide.
That is the cost of leaving it undecided: every week produces another design of the same surface, and answering them one at a time guarantees an inconsistent config vocabulary.

### #686 — the enforcement substrate

Filed as a proposal to adopt the `nono` sandbox, but the more useful reading is a question about what pi-permission-system fundamentally is.

Dependants: #694, #609, #680, #698, #706.

Five open items and three already-fixed escapes (#350, #481, #653) are the same defect class — static AST analysis cannot resolve runtime values, cannot see through `xargs` and `find -exec`, and cannot distinguish a read from a write.
`docs/configuration.md:590-592` already concedes this, describing Bash path extraction as best-effort and stating that variable expansion is not parsed.
The escapes are therefore not bugs against the design; they are the design's stated boundary being rediscovered one report at a time.

### #620 — the allow-capable adjudicator (ADR 0007 slice 2)

Answers #698 and most of #472 by reference.

Scheduling is deliberately deferred until #639 lands, because the two ADRs overlap on where adjudication sits in the policy model.

### Sequencing tension between #639 and #686

## 639 asks whether capabilities — reading versus writing paths, exec, net — should be first-class in policy

A capability-based sandbox is precisely what #686 proposes as the enforcement layer.
So #686 is an input to #639, not merely a downstream implementation choice, and deciding #639's capability vocabulary without it risks specifying a model the enforcement layer cannot express.
Rank order here is 8 then 9, but they should be decided together or with #686 read first.

### Findings that changed a rank

- **#694 verified on current `main`, not taken on assertion.**
  `expandHomePath` (`packages/pi-permission-system/src/expand-home.ts:17-27`) handles `~`, `~/`, `$HOME`, and `$HOME/` but has no `${HOME}` branch, and `classifyTokenAsPathCandidate` (`packages/pi-permission-system/src/access-intent/bash/token-classification.ts:52-61`) has no `$HOME/…` branch at all.
  Both gaps are structural, not incidental.
- **#704 verified on current `main`.**
  `cleanupWorktree`'s catch block calls `removeWorktree` — which is `git worktree remove --force` — and returns `{ hasChanges: false }` (`packages/pi-subagents-worktrees/src/worktree.ts:153-160`).
  The data loss is unconditional once the safety-net commit throws.
- **#694 is ranked high despite #686 possibly obsoleting it.**
  If the substrate changes, a variable-expansion fix is throwaway work.
  It is still ranked 2, because a live policy bypass cannot wait on an ADR — but the fix should be scoped narrowly for that reason, not built into elaborate machinery.
- **Seven PRs had never run CI at all.**
  `statusCheckRollup` was empty for #705, #703, #702, #697, #693, #692, and #675 — that is *not run*, not *passed*.
  Approving those runs changed three ranks: #692 and #675 turned out red on Fallow audit, and #702 red on Lint, none of which was visible before.
- **#613's premise does not hold.**
  It describes adding "the documented `defaultRunInBackground` global setting", but that string does not exist anywhere in `packages/pi-subagents/` outside historic plans and retros.
  This needs a question to the author, not a review.
- **Green checks are current, but three are approaching stale.**
  #690's green ran 2026-08-01 against files last changed 2026-07-28, so it is fresh.
  #684, #671, and #670 ran 2026-07-28; `packages/pi-permission-system/src` and the touched `pi-subagents` files have not changed since, so those greens still hold — but any permission-system merge invalidates #684 and #671 immediately.
- **#684's green is not an endorsement.**
  It widens who may approve `external_directory` access, and CI has no opinion about a widened security boundary.
  Its rank (17) reflects that it needs the authority model first.
- **No cross-package flake surfaced this run.**
  The pi-autoformat acceptance flake tracked in #678 was fixed on 2026-07-29 by isolating those tests into their own CI step, and no fork PR failed on an unrelated package.
- **#708 is accurate and partly upstream.**
  The root manifest does use `catalog:` specifiers, and npm rejects them regardless of `--omit=dev`, so `pi install git:` cannot work today.
  `packageManager: pnpm@11.5.2` is declared in `package.json:6`, so the reporter's suggested fix — detect the repository's package manager — is well-founded, but it belongs in Pi's installer.

### CI and security audit

Audited before approving any fork run, per the escalation-surface checklist.

| Check                                                                        | Result                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Privileged triggers (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`, `issue_comment`) | None; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` uses `push` to `main` and plain `pull_request` only                                                                    |
| `release-please` job (holds `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`, `contents: write`)       | Gated on `github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, unreachable from a fork ref                                                                                 |
| `publish` job (holds `id-token: write`)                                      | Gated on `needs.release-please.outputs.releases_created`, unreachable                                                                                   |
| Untrusted text in `run:` blocks                                              | None; no `github.event.*.body`, no `github.head_ref`; only `github.base_ref`, which GitHub constrains to a real base branch                             |
| `label-issues.yml`                                                           | `issues: write` only, triggered by `issues`, not by PRs                                                                                                 |
| PRs touching CI or install surfaces                                          | Two: #702 edits `packages/pi-permission-system/scripts/verify-public-types.sh`, which the `check` job runs; #692 adds a dependency and a lockfile entry |

Both sensitive diffs were read before approval.

### Open question recorded for the next run

The "pi-permission-system is not a sandbox" boundary is treated here as a **live open question**, not settled policy.
The evidence is the escape-report cadence: #350, #481, and #653 fixed, #694 open, and #686, #698, #706, #680 all asking for something the current substrate cannot deliver.
The next triage should check whether #686 has been decided, and if not, whether another escape has been filed in the interim — that count is the honest measure of the tax.
